title: Growth and Development (6-11 Years)
summary: From about 2½–3 years to 10 years children gain about 5–7 cm in height and 2–3 kg in weight a year. Growth spurt is the sudden increase in height and weight at 11–13 years; girls start earlier, so girls of 9–10 years are often taller than boys. Body proportions: the head is ¼ of the body at birth, about 1/6 at 6–8 years and 1/8 in adults. Teeth: 20 milk teeth at 3 years; 28 permanent teeth by middle childhood; 32 in adults. Bones: all are formed by middle childhood and have enough calcium to be strong, which is one reason for the high activity level. Muscles and fat: from 7–8 years girls gain more fat than muscle and boys more muscle than fat, so boys are generally stronger.

Muscular co-ordination is learnt control of muscles: gross co-ordination uses large muscles (running, balancing, skipping, climbing) and fine co-ordination uses small muscles of fingers and toes (writing, needlework, painting, picking a pencil). Gross co-ordination is learnt before fine. Sensitive period is the time when a specific skill is learnt most effectively; children should not be forced to write before four and a half to five and a half years. Skills by age: 6 years skip with two legs, balance on one foot briefly; 7 hop and jump in small squares; 8 skip with alternate hopping rhythm; 9 jump as high as oneself, hop on one foot for long; 10 run and jump hurdles, judge and stop a ball.

By middle childhood the basic command of language is complete; vocabulary of about 14,000 to 30,000 words; understand that one word can have more than one meaning and that words pronounced alike can have different spellings (here/hear, whole/hole); enjoy metaphors (bright as the sun), tongue twisters and jokes based on subtle meanings, building a sense of humour.

Social development is learning to behave in socially approved ways and get along with others; emotional development is gaining control over emotions and expressing them in socially approved ways. Parents: confident, democratic parents who accept their children as they are, set clear rules and praise good behaviour build self-confidence and self-esteem. Peer group (playmates of the same age): lets children compare themselves with others, gives emotional security and comfort adults cannot, teaches how to get along in society and makes children independent of parents (e.g. Rahul able to spend a night away from his mother). School: teachers encourage children and praise things done well so they develop self-confidence.

Cognitive development is the way a child thinks, reasons and solves problems; 6–11 years is a major turning point to logical thinking: differentiating fantasy from reality (Santa Claus), understanding another's point of view (empathy; inability to empathise is egocentrism), reversibility (thinking backwards through steps, e.g. mud ball to bed to snake), conservation (physical properties such as number or volume stay the same despite appearance: ten coins spread out, juice in tall and wide glasses), classification (sorting objects in many ways, e.g. playing cards), seriation (arranging in order: A taller than B and B taller than C, so A is taller than C) and concepts of time and speed. Cognitive development depends on heredity and environment; an enriched environment helps. All areas of development are inter-related.

objective: Look at two children. (i) A four-year-old is shown two lines of ten coins, one long (coins spread out) and one short, and says the long line has more coins. (ii) A ten-year-old is told A is taller than B and B is taller than C and says A is taller than C. Analyse the cognitive behaviour of each child.

(i) The four-year-old lacks conservation: he does not know that the number remains the same when coins are spread out. (ii) The ten-year-old shows seriation (logical ordering) and can reason correctly.

Identify two characteristics of language development in middle childhood. (a) Understanding that one word has more than one meaning (b) Having no vocabulary (c) Liking tongue twisters and metaphors (d) Unable to speak sentences.

Match the cognitive characteristic with the example. (a) Conservation (b) Seriation. Examples: (i) arranging bottles by height (ii) the same amount of drink in tall and wide glasses (iii) replying loudly.
State True or False. (a) Children of 6–11 years get confused between words that sound alike. (b) Peer group provides emotional security and comfort.
(a) False: they can differentiate them and enjoy using them. (b) True.
vsa: Explain the following characteristics of cognitive development in middle childhood with an example each: (i) conservation (ii) egocentrism (iii) seriation.

Conservation: knowing that ten coins stay ten however spread out. Egocentrism: a young child cannot see another's point of view, such as nodding to a mother who cannot see. Seriation: arranging bottles or sisters by height in order.
Why do girls of 9–10 years become taller than boys?
Girls begin their growth spurt earlier than boys. They reach the maximum earlier, so boys catch up later.
What is sensitive period? Give an example.
It is the time when the body is ready to learn a specific skill most efficiently. Children should not be forced to write before about five years because their fine muscles are not ready.
Give two differences between fine and gross muscular co-ordination.
Gross co-ordination uses large muscles, as in running and climbing. Fine co-ordination uses small muscles, as in writing or needlework, and is learnt later.
Why is the peer group important in middle childhood? Give two reasons.
It gives emotional security and comfort that adults cannot. It helps children compare themselves and become independent of parents.
sa: Describe the physical development in middle childhood (three points).

(i) Children gain about 5–7 cm in height and 2–3 kg in weight each year. (ii) The head becomes smaller in proportion to the body (about 1/6) and permanent teeth number 28. (iii) All bones are formed and strong, and boys have more muscle while girls have more fat.
How does the socio-emotional development of an 8-year-old differ from that of a 4-year-old? (three points)

(i) The 8-year-old controls emotions and expresses them in socially approved ways. (ii) He can understand another's point of view and cooperate with peers. (iii) He gains self-confidence from parents, peers and school, whereas a 4-year-old is egocentric and depends on parents.
Explain the language development of a 10-year-old (three points).

(i) A command of language is complete with a vocabulary of about 14,000 to 30,000 words. (ii) The child understands that one word can have many meanings and that similar sounding words have different spellings. (iii) The child enjoys metaphors, tongue twisters and jokes.
la: Describe the cognitive characteristics of a child of 11 years.

(i) The child differentiates between fantasy and reality. (ii) The child understands another's point of view (empathy) and is not egocentric. (iii) The child has reversibility, thinking backwards through steps. (iv) The child shows conservation of number, volume and mass. (v) The child classifies objects in many ways and arranges them in order (seriation). (vi) The child understands time and speed, such as which car reaches earlier.
